If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3120. President Donald Trump Claims He'll "Veto Everything" if Democrats Retake Congress, and It Has Big Implications for the Stock Market

Democrats are widely expected to retake one or both houses of Congress, creating potential friction points for Wall Street.

With mere hours left on Election Night before polling closes across America, traders on prediction market platform Polymarket are forecasting an 89% chance (as of 7 p.m. ET) that Democrats sweep and retake both the House of Representatives and the Senate. For context, Republicans enter the midterms with 218 of 435 House seats and 53 of 100 Senate seats.

The potential implications of midterm elections on the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.38%), S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.36%), and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.83%) are massive. If a "blue wave" does unfold, things could get dicey, at least over the short run, for a historically expensive stock market.

President Trump may soon be working with a divided government. Image source: Official White House Photo by Molly Riley.

President Donald Trump hasn't been keen on the prospect of working with the opposition. In a recent Fox News interview, he proclaimed that "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto" if a blue wave takes shape, and has previously gone on record as stating that he'd "veto everything" sent to him by a Democrat-led Congress.

On the one hand, the political gridlock that ensues from a divided Congress can, in some ways, be beneficial for the stock market. A split Congress effectively takes all major tax and spending legislation off the table, likely locking in historically low personal and corporate income tax rates through at least the end of Trump's presidency in January 2029. Wall Street loves when things are predictable.

"I guess I'll become Mr. Veto." President Trump lays out his strategy for dealing with a potential Democratic-controlled Congress in an exclusive interview with Miranda Devine. Trump says he would veto legislation before eventually negotiating compromises, while expressing hope Republicans maintain control after Tuesday's midterms.

At the same time, a non-unified government can create friction points for the stock market. For example, a Democrat-controlled Congress could make debt-ceiling negotiations far more challenging. The debt ceiling is forecast to be reached in the first half of 2027. If Democrats take one or both houses of Congress, the odds of a lengthy government shutdown rise.

We'd likely also see friction between President Trump and Democrats over artificial intelligence (AI) regulation. Whereas Trump favors as little regulation as possible for Wall Street's and the U.S. economy's No. 1 catalyst, most Democratic lawmakers prefer to limit data center expansion and impose tougher restrictions on AI solutions, including large language models.

Even if President Trump successfully vetoes AI legislation from a Democrat-controlled Congress, simply putting AI regulations in the spotlight could be bad news for stocks.

From a statistical standpoint, no political scenario is less desirable for investors than a Republican president overseeing a divided Congress. According to Retirement Researcher, the S&P 500's average annual return over 34 years is just 7.33% under this scenario, compared to 14.01% to 16.63% under the other political scenarios.

While this might sound less than ideal, a little historical perspective changes everything. For instance, the S&P 500 has been higher at the six- and 12-month mark following every midterm election over the last 75 years, with November up 100% of the time!

S&P 500 is higher 6 and 12 months after every midterm election over the last 75 years 📈🤑🥳 https://t.co/N1Eu0fZDie

Furthermore, a 7.33% average annual return, while notably lower than other political situations, is still markedly higher than the long-term annualized returns for real estate, commodities, and Treasury bonds. Even at their "worst," stocks have continued to shine brightest for those willing to be patient.

Even if President Trump's threats to "veto everything" perturb equities over the short term, history says that the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite are well-positioned for success, regardless of which political party is in power.

#3118. Why Fiserv Stock Triumphed on Tuesday

The company showed signs of a potential turnaround in its third-quarter earnings.

Fiserv (FISV +12.46%), one of the sturdier and more experienced fintechs on the market, had a Tuesday to remember as far as its equity was concerned. After it served up an encouraging quarterly earnings report in the morning, investors eagerly bought the company's shares to send them almost 13% higher across that trading session.

Fiserv's third-quarter revenue not under generally accepted accounting principles (non-GAAP, or adjusted) slid by 1% year over year to $4.85 billion. Despite the slide, that figure was essentially in line with the consensus analyst estimate.

As for profitability, adjusted net income fell more steeply, decreasing by 15% to $936 million, or $1.75 per share. Those Fiserv-tracking pundits were expecting a slightly sharper fall, since they were collectively estimating $1.72.

Fiserv said in its earnings release that the erosion in revenue it suffered in its key banking customer segment was improving notably. Clients didn't migrate away from Fiserv back-end solutions as much as they had in other recent quarters, while the company reported "major client wins" in that business.

Investors were also heartened by management's doubling of its Project Elevate cost-saving and automation target to $1 billion from $500 million. Another confidence booster was the company's news that it would resume its share repurchase program, with a goal of buying back $500 million worth of stock in the current (fourth) quarter alone.

Fiserv maintained its full-year 2026 organic revenue guidance of a slump of 1% to break-even when matched against the previous year's figure. It's also sticking to its adjusted EPS forecast of $7.20 to $7.40, which is well down from the $8.64 it posted in 2025.

While no investor likes to see declines in either trailing results or guidance, Fiserv's moves position it for renewed growth in the near future. So now feels like it might be an opportune time to buy into the company's (hopefully continuing) recovery story.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

#3116. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3115. Should You Buy Alphabet Stock After Anthropic Raised Its Google Commitment to $121 Billion?

The Claude maker just raised its minimum spending commitment to Google. Can it pay?

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind Claude, updated its initial public offering (IPO) filing on Monday, Nov. 2, adding its third-quarter results. On Sept. 30, it had $95.6 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $36.3 billion in short-term investments -- around $132 billion combined, near its total at the end of June.

Against this, Anthropic has signed purchase commitments and leases worth about $895.4 billion, almost all for compute and infrastructure. The first filing, on Oct. 26, left that figure blank.

And one of the largest parts goes to Alphabet (GOOGL +0.37%)(GOOG +0.08%). Anthropic now says it committed to spend at least about $121.3 billion with Google between April 2026 and July 2033, no matter how much it uses. Last week's filing had that number at about $114.5 billion.

With Alphabet shares near $283 as I write, is this durable revenue for Google Cloud, or a bet on a customer that lost money from operations last quarter? I think it's mainly the former over the next couple of years.

Google Cloud's revenue backlog (contracted revenue not yet recognized) hit $560.8 billion on Sept. 30. Three months earlier, it stood at $513.9 billion. And a year before, Alphabet's total backlog, mainly Google Cloud, was just $157.7 billion, under an older count that left out contracts for a year or less. But growth has slowed lately, with around $47 billion added in the third quarter versus almost $52 billion in the second.

Anthropic's $121.3 billion minimum equals around 22% of that cloud backlog. Alphabet doesn't say how much of the number comes from Anthropic, and some of the minimum has probably been spent since April. But it's a big share tied to one customer.

Spread across a bit more than seven years, the minimum averages around $16.5 billion a year. Google Cloud's third-quarter revenue climbed 103% year over year to $30.7 billion, a rate of around $123 billion a year. This puts Anthropic's average minimum at about 13% of the cloud unit's current sales -- important, but not the whole business.

Anthropic also estimates it could spend another $125 billion to $150 billion on Google's custom AI chips, though some of that might go through third-party providers rather than Google.

For the next year, Anthropic looks able to pay. Around $69.8 billion of its commitments are due in the 12 months after Sept. 30. Its cash and investments cover it almost twice, not counting $14.8 billion of credit it hasn't tapped or any proceeds from its IPO.

The business is helping. Third-quarter revenue climbed around 47% from the second quarter to about $17.0 billion, more than 12 times its revenue for the year-ago quarter. Multiply that by four, and it's close to what comes due in the next 12 months.

Operating cash flow for the first nine months of 2026 was a positive $6.6 billion, versus negative $2.0 billion for the same period of 2025.

But growth cooled from the second quarter's 144% sequential jump. Anthropic had a third-quarter operating loss of $567 million, which included around $2.0 billion of non-cash charitable contributions. A year before, it lost $3.1 billion.

Still, compute and infrastructure costs rose back to 58% of revenue in the third quarter, against 48% in the second, but they were 148% of revenue a year ago.

Later on, the bills get far bigger. Around $447.5 billion of the commitments are expected before the end of 2030 -- about $105 billion a year, well over Anthropic's current revenue pace.

"We must grow our customer base and expand revenue rapidly in order to generate the cash flows necessary to satisfy these commitments," Anthropic wrote in the filing.

If Anthropic spends less than its minimum, it must pay Google the difference. Of course, that payment only helps Google if Anthropic has the cash. And Google has agreed to provide up to $20 billion of financing, in convertible notes or stock, subject to conditions, so part of what Anthropic pays Google might come from Google itself.

Alphabet doesn't need Anthropic to work out perfectly for its stock to make sense. Shares trade at around 19 times expected 2027 earnings, about 31% under their 52-week high. And Google Cloud earned $11.1 billion of operating income in the third quarter, around three times the $3.6 billion it made a year before.

Does the amended filing change my take on Alphabet? Not much. But I'd treat the next few years of the Google commitment as solid revenue and the later years as a bet on Anthropic's growth.

Overall, I think Alphabet stock is still worth a look at this price.

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3113. Novartis: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Operating margins are on track to hit 40% by 2029 as cost discipline accelerates alongside new drug launches.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 27, 2026, Novartis (NVS -1.40%) raised its full-year 2026 core operating income guidance after delivering 4% net sales growth. This performance matters for long-term investors because the pharmaceutical giant is demonstrating that expanding sales from recently launched drugs can successfully replace revenue from older medicines losing patent protection. Three key insights from management explain how the company is maintaining its growth trajectory.

Novartis raised its full-year 2026 core operating income guidance, which tracks non-GAAP (adjusted) operating profit before one-time items, to in-line to low-single-digit growth, up from a previously projected decline. This operational shift shows that rising sales of priority medicines are offsetting patent expirations for key legacy treatments.

Management upgraded peak sales projections for key pipeline drugs, including Rhapsido for skin conditions such as chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), where hives appear without clear triggers. Promising trial results for remibrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS), a central nervous system disorder, further reinforce the company's ability to replace aging therapies.

Selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expenses, which cover marketing and operational overhead, fell 7% during the third quarter. Lower third-party spending and efficiency gains from technology are driving progress toward a target of 40% core operating margin by 2029.

Sales momentum across newly launched drugs is outpacing legacy revenue losses, and management is openly highlighting this replacement capability. The company benefits from commercial scale across international markets and a deep pipeline, while management tracks patent litigation outcomes and pricing discipline.

Capital allocation remains focused on steady dividend growth and targeted share repurchases, supported by free cash flow generation. The long-term thesis hinges on whether late-stage clinical readouts maintain this momentum over the coming years.

#3112. AI Is Making The App Optional

Haz Hubble is the Co-Founder and CEO at Pally (YC S25).

When I started building Pally, an AI assistant that keeps people on top of their messages, I assumed it needed its own app. We built one, with onboarding, settings and a home feed. Fewer than 20% of new users were still active in their second month.

We removed the app and moved the product into iMessage. Users now sign up by texting a number. With the same AI underneath, month-two retention rose to over 70%. That result made me question how much of consumer software exists only to support the app around it.

Every app asks people to do work before they get anything back. They have to find it, install it, create an account, learn where things are and remember that it exists. Some share of users gives up at each step.

The phone they’re installing it on is already crowded. The average user has more than 80 apps, and about 62% of them go unused in a given month. In the U.S., people spend around 80% of their app time in their three most-used apps. A new app is asking for a place that most people have stopped giving out.

The first is new hardware. OpenAI has said it will show its first consumer device, a screenless product designed with Jony Ive, in the second half of 2026. The last well-funded attempt, Humane’s AI Pin, failed. A common explanation is that it asked people to change their habits without giving them enough reason to.

The second is the super-app. WeChat hosts more than 4.3 million mini-programs, and roughly 764 million people used them each day in 2025. People in China order food and pay bills through services they never downloaded, because those services sit inside an app they already open all day. The model depends on one company controlling the platform, which is part of why nothing comparable exists in the U.S.

The third is putting AI inside the messaging apps people already use, such as iMessage, SMS, WhatsApp and email. Language models make this practical because a conversation can now do the job that buttons and menus used to do. The assistant can also message first, so users don’t have to remember to open anything. Of the three approaches, this is the only one that doesn’t ask people to form a new habit.

Satya Nadella made a version of this argument about business software in December 2024. He said, “The notion that business applications exist will probably collapse” as AI agents take on more work. He reasoned that most apps are databases with rules on top, and agents can apply those rules on a user’s behalf.

The same reasoning applies to consumer products. When an assistant can read your messages, check your calendar and act on a request written in plain English, many of an app’s screens become optional. Messaging is where this shows up first, because it’s where people already spend their attention.

Building inside another company’s messaging app means that company can shut you out. Meta did exactly that in January 2026, when WhatsApp stopped allowing general-purpose AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity on its business platform. After EU regulators intervened, Meta restored access in the European Economic Area in July. As of late July, the ban had not been lifted in the U.S.

Apple’s position is different. In June 2025, a federal judge refused to dismiss the Justice Department’s antitrust case against Apple, and the allegations the court let stand include restrictions on iMessage and on super-apps. Apple has reportedly made several settlement offers to the DOJ this year. While that case is open, blocking third-party assistants from iMessage would hand regulators a fresh example of the conduct they’re already suing over.

That doesn’t resolve the risk. Apple could still change its rules, and no messaging platform has made a lasting commitment to AI developers. Anyone building this way should plan for losing a channel.

1. Within five years, most consumer apps will work mainly as back-ends. Their data and logic will still matter, but people will reach them through an assistant instead of opening them.

2. A phone number will replace the App Store listing as the way many people first try a new product.

3. Screens will be generated when a task needs one, such as signing a contract or reading a chart, and will close when the task is done.

4. Consumer products will be judged by completed tasks. Time spent in an app will start to look like a cost to the user.

5. Regulators will treat AI access to messaging platforms the way they treated browser choice and app store rules, and at least one major platform will be required to open up to third-party assistants in the U.S.

If you’re building a consumer product today, make three changes.

• Track how long a new user takes to get value, counted in messages rather than screens. If the first exchange doesn’t help them, fix that before anything else.

• Build the version with no interface first. Add screens only where text doesn’t work, such as payments or reviewing long documents.

• Keep your data and logic on your own infrastructure, so you can move between iMessage, SMS, WhatsApp and email if a platform changes its rules.

For Pally, this means treating iMessage as our first channel, not our only one. We keep the product’s logic on our own infrastructure so it can run over SMS, WhatsApp or email if Apple’s rules change. We add a screen only when a user can’t finish a task in text, and every new feature has to work without asking anyone to open something new.

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.

#3109. BigBear.ai vs. Nebius: Which AI Stock Is the Better Buy for 2027?

One of these AI stocks is shrinking and losing money, while the other is growing at triple digits and just turned profitable.

As the artificial intelligence (AI) race intensifies, investors are looking beyond the biggest names for hidden opportunities. Deciding between BigBear.ai (BBAI -1.94%) and Nebius Group (NBIS +7.25%) requires weighing government contracts against cloud infrastructure.

BigBear.ai focuses on decision-intelligence software for high-stakes defense environments. Nebius builds the actual full-stack infrastructure needed to train and deploy these complex models. While both companies operate in the fast-moving AI sector, their business models, financial health, and customer bases offer investors starkly different paths.

BigBear.ai provides specialized decision-intelligence and autonomy software tailored for government and commercial sectors. It provides biometric and data analysis solutions, with a major concentration of contracts adding a layer of risk.

On a trailing-12-month (TTM) basis through the June quarter, revenue reached nearly $142 million, which represents a decline of approximately 1.5% compared to the prior year.

The company reported a net loss of close to $180 million. This performance indicates that expenses significantly exceeded total sales.

As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 4.9x, measuring the ability to cover short-term debts with current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was 0, as the company carries no debt.

TTM free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was negative $73 million, indicating the business consumes more cash than it generates.

Nebius Group positions itself as an AI cloud company, building the full-stack infrastructure required for complex machine learning tasks. Its platform supports AI builders across healthcare and financial services by offering tools for model training and deployment. The company operates a global footprint with data centers and roughly 400 AI engineers to maintain its competitive position.

As of the June quarter, TTM revenue reached nearly $1.4 billion, representing a significant 444% year-over-year increase. Net income improved to $62 million, up from under $10 million for the full year 2025. This performance shows a swing to profitability following significant net losses in previous years, driven by high demand for cloud services.

Based on its June 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 4.0x, while the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 1.0x. The company's total debt was approximately $8.6 billion, with an additional $1.5 billion in lease liabilities. This was partially offset by $8 billion of cash and equivalents.

TTM free cash flow was negative $5.9 billion, reflecting the capital-intensive nature of the company's AI infrastructure. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 21.6% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation because it is a non-cash expense.

BigBear.ai faces significant risks from revenue concentration, as a large portion of its business depends on a limited number of government contracts. These agreements are subject to budgetary fluctuations and may be terminated at any time for convenience.

Nebius is funding massive capital spending needs. Heavy capital investment for data centers has resulted in negative free cash flow, and a slowdown in AI demand remains the primary risk.

BigBear.ai appears cheaper based on sales over the past twelve months, while Nebius is the only one with a positive forward P/E using future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

I would buy Nebius over BigBear right now. BigBear has a multi-year history of flat revenue. It reported $146 million in revenue in 2021, and $128 million in 2025. It has reported a net loss across that period. The company has to compete for government contracts, while Nebius has seen its revenue explode due to a shortage of data center capacity and high demand.

Nebius is seeing immediate demand for its infrastructure as soon as it is brought online. Additionally, Nebius benefits from pricing power, with recent bids for compute capacity fetching higher prices than before.

Analysts expect BigBear to continue reporting losses over the next few years, while expecting Nebius to continue growing earnings over the long term as it brings more capacity online.

The risk for Nebius is that the stock trades at high multiples of sales and earnings. A lot of growth is priced in, so anything that stalls the AI build-out could hurt the stock. The stock has already fallen 38% in the last month over concerns about AI spending.

Still, Nebius has a scarce asset that is in high demand, and that scarcity is being validated by explosive revenue growth and improving profitability. That's the stock I would rather hold for 2027 and beyond.

#3108. AI Pods Are Redefining The Unit Of Software Delivery

Alexey Spas is the founder and CEO of Instinctools, a software engineering company focused on AI-powered digital solutions.

For most of the software industry’s history, when a software backlog started growing faster than the team could handle it, a CTO or product leader knew what came next. It was either opening new roles or sending some work to an outside partner.

Whichever the option, the rule of thumb used to be the same: More software to build meant more people needed to build it, until AI put that long-held assumption into question.

A senior engineer working with coding agents can now produce far more raw output than before. That is why software delivery is beginning to reorganize around a different unit: a small senior team surrounded by AI-enabled workflows.

The label is still loose, but the operating idea is easy to picture: An AI pod is a compact, senior-led engineering team accountable for a defined software outcome. Specialized AI agents support the delivery flow from requirements drafting to code generation and testing, while humans keep their hands on the wheel when it comes to business context, quality, security and the final result.​​

And just like that, AI has completely reshuffled the deck for software engineering. An age-old dilemma is now taking on new contours: If companies need a different kind of delivery unit, where should it live? Some organizations will have good reasons to build it in-house. Others may prefer to bring in an external pod. For many, the most practical answer may sit somewhere in between.​

A big part of the appeal of an in-house AI pod is its lean structure, and it’s not hard to see why: Hiring one or two senior engineers supported by AI agents is a very different proposition from building a cross-functional team of five-plus people.

The strongest case for keeping the pod internal, though, may have less to do with headcount than with proximity of in-house engineers to the product, business context and the decisions. Moreover, the lessons learned while building AI-enabled delivery workflows remain inside the organization.

That advantage takes time to build. Giving experienced developers access to coding agents does not immediately produce an effective AI delivery system. Teams still have to determine what can safely be delegated, where human review belongs, which quality gates can be automated and how AI-generated work fits into the rest of the software lifecycle.

There is also the expertise question. A small pod can still draw on a broad range of skills. A modernization effort can suddenly require security input, an AI-heavy feature may call for data engineering or a customer-facing workflow may need experienced UX support. Building all of those competencies internally makes sense when the demand is sustained. It is harder to justify when the need appears for only a few weeks.​

There is no secret AI stack tool available only to software vendors. Anyone can access the same models, coding assistants and agentic frameworks. The advantage of an external pod usually comes from reducing the distance between access to AI and a delivery system that works.

If spinning up a few agents could solve the software delivery problem overnight, things would be simple. In practice, faster generation creates its own downstream load: More code has to be reviewed, tested, integrated and checked for security. The challenge is turning that AI-driven speed into production-ready software.

An outsourced team that has already cut its teeth on different projects can bring patterns refined across more than one production environment: agent configurations, evaluation methods, review workflows, reusable components and quality controls. I know—there’s a lot of skepticism when software development vendors talk about their “unique expertise.” But in this case, uniqueness does not mean exclusive knowledge that nobody else can acquire. It just implies a shorter route through mistakes someone else has already made and experience that has been tested often enough to become adaptable.

There is also a flip side to that breadth of experience. An external pod does not begin with the same institutional knowledge as an internal team, nor is it naturally as close to every product decision. The model makes the most sense when the value of faster ramp-up, cross-project experience or temporary capacity outweighs the benefits of having a team deeply embedded in the product.​

When a company needs AI-enabled delivery capability now but is not yet certain how much of it should become a fixed part of the organization, a hybrid model can be considered. Demand may surge around a product launch, modernization program or backlog push, and then ease again. An external pod can take the edge off this sudden spike without turning peak capacity into permanent headcount.

The same arrangement can also serve a longer-term purpose. A company that ultimately wants the capability in-house can use an outsourced pod as a working prototype for the team it may later build itself.

A “borrow, prove, then build” approach gives leaders a chance to observe which roles they repeatedly need, which workflows survive production, where human judgment remains essential and which metrics genuinely improve. The parts that prove strategic can then move inside the organization with much less guesswork.​

AI pods are making the old build-versus-buy decision more nuanced. For leaders, the choice comes down to a few practical questions: How enduring is the demand? How important is institutional knowledge? How quickly should the capability become operational?

The answers may change as the organization learns. That is probably the main point. AI is reshaping software delivery quickly enough that the operating model that fits today does not have to be the one a company commits to for good.​​

#3107. Nike vs. Procter & Gamble: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Nike trades at a premium valuation despite slowing growth, while P&G's defensive portfolio offers a contrasting risk-return profile.

Investors often weigh the potential of iconic growth brands against the stability of essential household names. Deciding between Nike (NKE -1.64%) and Procter & Gamble (PG -0.92%) means choosing between athletic innovation and daily necessity.

Nike serves the athletic world with footwear and apparel, leveraging a massive digital presence to reach global fans. Procter & Gamble offers a defensive shield with brands like Tide and Gillette. These companies represent different strategies for long-term growth and capital preservation in a shifting economic landscape.

Nike designs and sells athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment across the globe through its own digital channels and a network of wholesale partners. The company operates primarily in the retail stocks space, focusing on high-performance gear and lifestyle products. In its latest annual report, filed for the period ending May 31, 2026, the company noted that its three largest U.S. customers accounted for approximately 29% of sales. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $46.4 billion. This performance follows a period of higher sales in earlier years, as the company reported approximately $51.4 billion in revenue during FY 2024. Net income for the most recent year was $3.1 billion.

Procter & Gamble manufactures branded consumer packaged goods across diverse categories, including Fabric & Home Care, Baby Care, and Beauty. The company sells to mass merchandisers, grocery stores, and drug stores, reaching billions of consumers worldwide. Walmart (WMT -2.22%) and its affiliates represent approximately 16% of total sales, which indicates a notable reliance on a single major retail partner. This focus on essential goods helps the company maintain a steady presence throughout the globe.

In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $87 billion, which represents a growth rate of approximately 3.3% over the prior year. Net income for the period was nearly $16 billion. This performance highlights the ability of Procter & Gamble to maintain stable earnings and profit levels even as revenue fluctuates across its various global markets.

Nike faces intense competition in the athletic footwear and apparel market from rivals like Adidas (ADDDF -1.81%), Lululemon Athletica (LULU -0.82%), Under Armour (UAA +1.53%), V.F. (VFC +3.35%), and ASICS (ASCCF -7.79%). The company also competes with Li Ning (LNNGF +0.00%) and other international brands. Dependence on a concentrated base of contract manufacturers, primarily in Vietnam, Indonesia, and China, creates supply chain and disruption risks. Global economic volatility and currency fluctuations also significantly impact consumer spending and operational margins.

Procter & Gamble operates in a highly competitive consumer products industry with global and local rivals and private-label brands. The company is vulnerable to global supply chain disruptions, including commodity and raw material cost fluctuations and the impact of climate change. Macroeconomic and geopolitical instability, including trade controls and sanctions in countries where it operates, pose ongoing threats.

Procter & Gamble offers a more conservative valuation relative to its earnings estimates, while NIKE carries a higher price tag despite slower recent revenue growth.

Nike intrigues me as it moves away from being more of a growth stock toward a dividend stock. While this isn't often talked about, it has increased its dividend payouts for 24 consecutive years. That doesn't make it a Dividend King yet, as it would need to increase those payouts for 50 consecutive years, but it's on the path to becoming one. In addition to that consistency, the yield for that dividend is hefty, sitting at 4.1%.

The catch with Nike, however, is that sales are slumping, and some of the market may still be waiting for it to return to its high-growth ways. That mismatch between what Nike was and what it's becoming is where I see the investable opportunity. In the meantime, the stock price could continue to decline until sales stabilize, cutting into those dividend returns. That's why, between the two, I would rather own Procter & Gamble. While Nike is on the track to becoming a Dividend King, Procter already is one, having increased its payouts for 70 consecutive years.

With its essential household goods, it has also fared better than Nike thus far in 2026; Procter & Gamble shares are up 14.1%, while Nike's stock price is down 38.6%. And while Procter's dividend yield of 2.6% may be lower than Nike's yield, you aren't dealing with a stock price trying to get out of a rut.

#3104. There's a 99% Chance That Democrats Retake the House, and History Says This Shift Will Have a Huge Impact on Stocks

Nearly a century of S&P 500 return data shows that a worst-case scenario is likely to unfold -- but this isn’t the complete story.

Throughout the day, Americans from across our great nation have headed to the polls or mailed in their ballots to make their voices heard. According to popular prediction market Kalshi, as of 8:50 p.m. ET, the odds have skyrocketed to better than 99% that Democrats will retake control of the House of Representatives. Regardless of what happens in the Senate, President Trump would be working with a divided Congress come January 2027.

Based on what history tells us, a split Congress can significantly alter annualized return expectations for the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.38%), S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.36%), and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.83%).

President Trump will likely be working with a divided Congress in the new year. Image source: Official White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian.

If prediction markets prove accurate and Democrats do retake one or both houses of Congress, President Donald Trump's second nonconsecutive term will mirror his first. He'll have had two years of full Republican congressional control in the first half of each term, and a divided Congress in the second half of both.

To some extent, congressional division is welcome by Wall Street. Political gridlock makes it virtually impossible to pass major tax and spending legislation. In other words, personal and corporate income tax law should remain unchanged for the foreseeable future.

DEMOCRATIC SWEEP? UBS SEES 50% ODDS. UBS assigns a 50% probability to Democrats winning both chambers, while prediction markets put Democratic control of the House at 94% and Senate at 77%. UBS warns a sweep could complicate Trump's fiscal agenda and 2027 debt-ceiling negotiations, while tariffs and AI investment remain largely insulated.

But a congressional shake-up does have its sticking points. For instance, debt-ceiling negotiations would be far more challenging. Additionally, Trump's desire to minimize the regulation of artificial intelligence would clash with Democratic lawmakers who favor much tougher oversight of the stock market's top catalyst.

However, the biggest worry for investors comes from nearly a century of historical return data. A few years ago, online retirement planning site Retirement Researcher examined the average annual return of the S&P 500 from 1926 through 2023 under four political scenarios, yielding one outlier:

Statistically, no political scenario has produced less desirable returns for stock investors than what's expected to unfold on Election Night. But this also isn't the complete story.

While nearly a century of data points to lower average annual returns for the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite during President Trump's final two years in the White House, investors are in better shape than this data suggests.

For starters, a 7.33% average annual return still (pardon the apropos pun) trumps the long-term average annual return of other major asset classes, such as commodities, real estate, and Treasury bonds.

These next six months are historically the best of the year, but they are even better in a midterm year. In fact, 19 for 19 times we've seen November - April higher when starting in a midterm year. Will this time be different? https://t.co/kebp03JxpR

Furthermore, Carson Group's Chief Market Strategist, Ryan Detrick, notes that the six months following midterm elections have historically been exceptionally generous to investors since 1950, with November higher 19 of 19 times. In fact, the S&P 500 hasn't been down in the six- or 12-month period following a midterm election over the last 75 years.

In other words, even though history shows that near-term returns may be tempered a bit as President Trump and a divided Congress learn to work together, the long-term outlook for the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite remains as bright as ever.

#3101. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3100. The ERP Migration Blind Spots That Technology Alone Can't Fix

Bruno Billy, President & CEO of APGAR North America, advises organizations on the operational reality of data and enterprise transformation.

Enterprise resource planning (ERP) transformations remain high on the agenda for many large organizations. Mergers and acquisitions, consolidation and modernization are driving significant investment. For SAP customers, the approaching end of mainstream ERP Central Component (ECC) support adds further urgency.

But replacing an ERP is much more than replacing technology. It affects nearly everything about how a company does business, from processing customer orders to managing its supply chain and reporting financial results. The scope makes it notoriously difficult and expensive to execute.

The expense creates enormous pressure to get moving. Teams responsible for different workstreams often start before the organization agrees on how the new ERP should represent the business. Often, those differences start with the most basic assumptions about how the business operates.

Here’s a simple question that comes up surprisingly often during ERP transformations: what is a customer?

The obvious answer is the person or organization purchasing your products or services. Simple enough, right? But consider a manufacturer that sells through distributors. For finance, the customer might be the distributor that places the order and pays the invoice. For service, it might be the business actually using the product. Neither is wrong. Both definitions serve legitimate business needs.

An ERP needs to accommodate these nuances through its business objects, relationships and hierarchies. If implementation teams decide how to represent customers independently, they risk embedding conflicting assumptions in data mappings, system configurations and business processes.

Those conflicts may not become apparent until integration testing or financial reconciliation. By then, resolving them can require substantial rework, increase project costs, delay go-live and potentially disrupt business operations.

You won’t resolve every business requirement before an ERP migration begins, but there are three decisions I’d recommend making before the teams get too far into configuration and data migration.

Start by agreeing on how the business will be represented in the new ERP. For each major data domain, define the business entities, their relationships and the hierarchies needed to support operations and reporting.

This is particularly important when consolidating systems following an acquisition. In one organization I worked with, acquisitions had left the business operating six different ERP environments, each with its own representations of customers, suppliers and products. Supplier records in separate systems, for instance, may refer to subsidiaries of the same parent company. The future-state model should preserve those relationships so procurement can understand total spending across the supplier organization and negotiate accordingly.

Before approving the model, test it against actual legacy records. Can the migration team determine what each record becomes, which hierarchy it belongs to and how it relates to other entities? If the answers differ depending on who you ask, more business-design work is needed.

Not every difference needs to disappear. Some reflect legitimate regional or business-unit requirements. Not every local variation is inefficiency. Some may actually reflect a competitive advantage.

A manufacturer may sell the same product in several countries while using different packaging or meeting different regulatory requirements in each market. I find it useful to distinguish between what should be written in ink and what can be written in pencil.

• Write in ink the definitions, identities and relationships that need to remain consistent across the enterprise.

• Write in pencil the attributes and classifications that must accommodate local requirements.

Make these decisions with future rollouts in mind. The first implementation often establishes conventions that subsequent regions are expected to follow. A model designed exclusively around the first region’s needs can become an expensive constraint on everyone else.

Decide which systems are responsible for maintaining master data and, equally important, who has the authority to make decisions about it.

A customer record might originate in the CRM, while finance maintains credit information and payment terms. Authority may therefore need to be defined at the attribute or business-process level rather than assigned fully to one system. For each major data domain, identify who can create records, approve changes, resolve conflicts and authorize exceptions.

Consider a customer changing its legal name. Who determines whether that requires updating an existing record or creating a new legal entity? If CRM and finance reach different conclusions, the ERP can end up with conflicting information even when both systems are functioning correctly.

Establish these governance processes before go-live and sustain them afterward. Customers merge, suppliers reorganize and businesses expand. Without ownership and change management, the fragmentation you worked to eliminate will quickly return.

It is understandable to worry that business-model discussions will slow an already demanding program, but these decisions must be made eventually. The longer they are deferred, the more configuration, mappings and processes are built on assumptions that may need to be revisited.

Making the decisions early reduces rework and gives implementation teams a common foundation. It also creates value beyond the migration itself. The same business definitions and hierarchies can support reporting, analytics, future acquisitions and even AI applications.

An ERP doesn’t merely store your business’s data. It encodes a model of your business. If you haven’t agreed on that model before implementation starts, the implementation will make those decisions for you. ​

TL;DR: Mortgage rates kicked off the week with a drop, but they’re still above 7%.

Mortgage rates are cooling off as we roll into November. However, they’re still above the 7% threshold.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.07% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and 13 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

This week’s employment data could potentially push mortgage rates one way or the other — more on that below the graph.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

This week, the Nerds will be watching the October jobs report, which comes out on Friday, Nov. 6. If it shows that employment remained steady (or even improved), that will build a stronger case for the Federal Reserve to raise overnight borrowing rates again at their next meeting on Dec. 8-9.

While the Fed doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set the federal funds rate, which is the fee that banks must pay to borrow from one another (which is how they fund mortgages). Lenders raise mortgage rates any time they think that the federal funds rate is about to go up.

Central bankers hiked the federal funds rate in September, so a relatively steady jobs report would suggest the labor market could withstand higher rates.

The Fed has a dual mandate to control inflation while supporting maximum employment, and raising the federal funds rate is their main tool for bringing inflation down. If they can work to lower inflation without hurting employment too badly, central bankers may feel more confident to act.

The September Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE), the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, was released last Thursday. The data shows inflation was 3.6% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August.

September’s federal funds rate hike came in the middle of the month, so October’s inflation data will really capture its effect on inflation. The October PCE report will come out on Nov. 25.

#3094. Smithfield: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Smithfield's pivot to outsourced hog production and brand ownership cuts capital risk while packaged meats delivers steady cash flow.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 27, 2026, Smithfield (SFD -0.81%) reported an adjusted operating profit of $145 million, down from $310 million a year earlier as hog oversupply crushed upstream margins. High feed and transport costs hurt live animal production, but packaged meats generated stable cash flow and expanded margins. Three things management said stand out.

Smithfield signed a supply agreement to cut its internal hog production -- its upstream live-animal farming operations -- by 900,000 head per year. Shifting live-animal production to external partners reduces capital intensity while preserving processing volume.

The consumer products division -- which transforms fresh pork into bacon, sausage, and lunch meat -- expanded operating margin by 80 basis points to 11.6%. Smithfield outperformed rivals by taking volume share in its five largest retail categories.

Smithfield finalized its acquisition of Nathan's Famous, ending a licensing agreement that was set to expire in 2032. Owning the brand outright eliminates license royalty fees and opens up direct sales in food service channels.

Pork commodity oversupply continues to depress processing spreads, but steady consumer demand for packaged meats gives Smithfield cash flow to fund long-term growth. Management is watching export volume recovery and pricing discipline across retail channels.

With net debt at 0.5 times adjusted earnings, the balance sheet provides flexibility to maintain dividend payments through cyclical downturns.
